doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Live at the Jazz Workshop, This Here and live recording
summary: The San Francisco live album was his first hit, helped by all-night DJs, and showed the appeal of live jazz recording.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Well the one record too that was from right here in San Francisco I believe, where you had the idea to keep his crowd talk on the record.

Well that was part of the first live date that we did with him and it became a signature thing. That was the first breakthrough record and the first hit record that I ever had, actually, The Cannonball Adderley Quintet in San Francisco was “Live at the Jazz Workshop,” which was for many years a famous jazz club in this town. And that was actually, like all good hit albums, was propelled by one song really. It had Bobby Timmons’ “This Here” which became an incredibly well put — it was funny, that was about a twelve minute long track and you know where you’re not supposed to get it — but what we discovered was see in jazz at that point, as we’re going from the 50s into the 60s, a lot of the radio strength of jazz was in those all night disc jockeys, the guys that were on from before midnight into the dawn and stuff, like Symphony Sid in New York, like Sid McCoy in Chicago, and in most cases, because these guys were operating on clear channel 50,000 watt stations which lots of other stations went off the air in the

middle of the night, you could hear them forever. I think if you were being played by Symphony Sid in New York and by Sid McCoy out of WCFL I guess in Chicago, you could be heard practically everywhere. And these guys loved long numbers because they could then take a break, have a sandwich, go to the bathroom, whatever. I mean they loved twelve minute tunes. So the juxtaposition worked very well indeed. And that was I guess if my first artistic break was Monk, my second and my first commercial break was the Cannonball record, which really put us and him on the map in a lot of ways. And it’s interesting because that record, it established the label, it established the artist, I think it also did a hell of a lot, and I don’t know whether this is good or bad, but just the whole concept of live recording of jazz, not just that there hadn’t been such records before but this was a monster hit and a live record and it just, that whole idea of being able to catch and transfer the atmospherics of it, that whole excitement, the live ambience of the jazz performance in the jazz club and the audience reaction and such. It was a turning point there also. And you’ve got to remember, the other thing is when you’re recording, in those days, it’s not later when we get into the multi-track period and recording live means parking a truck outside which is really like a mobile control room and multi-track machines in the truck and they run the cable into the room, by contrast what we would basically do is set up in a corner someplace, it’s like we were in the two track days at this time, with a portable Ampex machine and hope that — there are lines going to our machines from the bandstand, and hope that — what happened one night I remember in a live recording at the old Five Spot was a customer kicked one of our cables and the plug came out of the wall and that was the end of that take. But you hope that didn’t happen too often. So to get good records out of that was a lot of fun and a lot of work too.
